recent approval decides, not any approval ever.

Registered agents, most recently registered first, with the total.

Each carries its version count and its latest version's content hash, so
the list view can show "what's actually running" without a second
round trip per row.

Now the same `{agents, shown, total, limit, offset}` shape `/datasets`
uses, for real page controls rather than a "show more" that only ever
grows the same list -- a deliberate break from this endpoint's own
former bare-array response, made because the console-wide pagination
pass this is part of asked for one consistent shape everywhere, not
because the earlier reasoning for keeping it bare was wrong at the
time. `useAgents()` and the two tests that read this response directly
(`activation.spec.ts`, `real-auth.spec.ts`) were updated in the same
change.

For data engineers and platform administrators.

post.description:
Register an agent, and its own runtime identity along with it.

No version yet, so nothing can run as this agent until one is
registered. Nothing picks an *existing* identity to run as any more:
the workload directory row is created here, named after this agent, in
the same transaction as the agent row itself, so neither can exist
without the other. `directory.id` is one global primary key across
every tenant (see `infra/postgres/seed-canary.sql`'s own comment on
this), which is why the id is tenant-prefixed rather than derived from
the name alone: two different tenants naming an agent the same thing
must not collide on one directory row.

Sharing an identity between two agents is exactly the failure this
closes. It means their tool calls cannot be told apart in the audit log,
and a lease granted for one silently covers the other too.

`approve_lease` uses, and for the same reason.

The graph's state is not held in a waiting process while a human decides:
it sits in the checkpointer's Postgres tables, so a run can be approved
days after it paused, by somebody who was not there when it started.

Stream an uploaded version's code archive back, for the worker only.

Gated by a shared secret rather than a directory identity, because the
caller is the worker process itself, not a person or a registered
agent principal, so "who in the tenant's directory is this" does not
apply to it. This endpoint is never reachable from `agentnet`: the
sandboxed containers a version's code eventually runs inside have no
route to this API at all except `POST /credentials`, a different
endpoint entirely.

How locking was used in the caller's organisation, for locked columns and locked files.

Without `section`, the latest lines of every list: reads and refusals, key uses, leases, contract treatments, erasures, and the opening of locked files.
With `section` (reads, column_leases, file_reads, file_leases, keys, erasures, small_groups or contracts), one list a page at a time, newest first, narrowed by
`person`, `table`, `file` (part of a file name), `date_from` and `date_to` (date and time; to is exclusive), `result` and `q`, with the number of lines that match. Each list accepts only
some of the filters, and says which.

For the privacy auditor and the data protection officer. Never a name, a value, a file name or an identifier.

get.description:
Prove the mechanism: a real session resolves to a real directory row.

Nothing downstream reads this endpoint yet. It exists so the login flow
can be verified end to end (console logs in, calls this, sees its own
identity come back) before anything is wired to depend on it.

The Munitas client library this platform offers: its version, the file to install, and the checksum of that file.

Open to anyone who can reach the platform, because `pip` cannot sign in. `path` is where the file is downloaded from, relative to the platform's address; install it
with `pip install <the platform's address><path>`. `sha256` is the checksum of exactly that file, for anyone who wants to check what they downloaded. When the
library was not built into this platform, `available` is false and nothing else is returned.
Download the client library as the file `pip` installs. Only the file this platform offers (named in `GET /client`) can be downloaded; any other name is not found.

post.description:
Mint a storage credential for one dataset version, or refuse and say why.

The order of operations matters and is not negotiable: decide, record the
decision, then act on it. File after acting would lose the audit trail
for exactly the requests that fail partway.

Three outcomes: 200 with the key when access is allowed and in effect,
403 when it is refused, and 202 when it is allowed but the storage
permissions could not be updated yet. A 202 is never a refusal: the
activator finishes the job and resumes a run that parked on it.

get.description:
Versions across all datasets, filterable by current class.

Filtering on `current_class` rather than the sealed class is deliberate:
the question people ask is "what is published right now", not "what was
sealed as published", and answering the second when they meant the first would
under-report exposure.

schema.title: Response List Versions Dataset Versions Get

post.description:
Seal a new dataset version.

A version is sealed on creation, which is why there is no update endpoint: a change is always a new version. The storage prefix encodes
organisation, dataset and version and never the class, so a later promotion changes a grant and moves no bytes.

A version that names a records file is also written as an Iceberg table, before the row exists. A small one is written while the request
waits. A large one is written by a worker, in a job: the answer is then 202 with the job, the version number and folder are reserved, and the
version is sealed, with its table inside it, when the job finishes. `table_mode` chooses; left out, the size of the records file does.

Only the platform's own workers may call this (the worker token). It names the organisation in its body, so a caller that could reach it
without proving what it is could seal a version into any organisation. A person's data arrives through the upload endpoint, which seals
under their session.

get.description:
One version, with the fields a detail screen needs.

`version_class` deliberately carries only the class question. The name,
content hash and record count are joined in here rather than added to the
view, because widening the view would make every caller pay for columns most
of them ignore, and the view's single purpose is what makes it trustworthy.

The organisation comes from the caller's session (`auth.organisation_scope`), never from
the URL, and a version belonging to another is **not found** rather than forbidden. That
distinction is the point: 403 confirms the version exists, which is half of what somebody
probing ids was trying to learn. The platform's own workers send the worker token instead
and name the organisation they act for. This endpoint also returns `object_manifest`, the
storage keys of the version's files, so it must never answer without one or the other.

A version made from a file somebody brought in also says so (`brought_in`): the file's name, its size and
its SHA-256, who sent it (`who`, and `who_label` with the person's name) and when. It is null for a version nothing was brought in for, such as one a
pipeline made.

itself. Narrowed to `custodian` for the same reason `/lease-requests` is,

only approver is in nobody's queue until the department has a second
approver, because nobody else may confirm it.

`verified_source` is never granted here, even when `source_kind` names HuggingFace, because that would trust a label the caller supplied.
The basis is upgraded later by `fetch_huggingface`, and only once the platform has made the request itself and can show the origin. The

licence and overwrites it, just as `declared_class` stays provisional until a custodian confirms it.

a mistake cannot be undone, but a refusal seals nothing, which makes
pressing this the check. A second Check button would ask the same question
and say the same thing twice.

Every problem is reported together. Reporting only the first would turn
twelve problems into twelve attempts.

know what an uploaded file is. This path does know, because the upload
endpoint read the audio, so it can claim audio_raw honestly rather than
asserting a shape nothing checked.

post.description:
Seal a table from two files: the privacy contract (YAML or JSON) and the rows.

The rows are a CSV or TSV with a header, a JSON list of rows, or a JSONL file with one row per line; the ending of the file's name says which,
with .gz or .zst after it for a compressed file. A CSV is read with the delimiter and encoding it declares (`delimiter`, `encoding`), with or
without a header (`header`), and the words that mean a missing value (`null_values`, separated by commas; an empty field by default).
Pressing this is the check: when anything is wrong in either file, nothing is sealed and every problem is listed together, each naming
its row, its line and its column. Values are read as the types the contract declares, strictly. A table about people sealed here is at most 20,000 rows
and 5 MB; an ordinary table is at most 5 MB. Larger tables are sealed another way.

A contract that names how to find the person each row is about seals a table of people, with the identifying columns locked under each
person's own key. A contract that says the table cannot be erased and names nobody seals an ordinary table, with nothing locked, that can be
queried like any other; the answer then carries `"plain": true` and no people. Either way the version starts at the most restricted level.

Start bringing in a table that is not about people, from a file too large for the table route, sent in parts of 8 MB.

The contract is checked and the file's name and size are accepted or refused before anything is sent. The upload reserves the next version
of the dataset, so a long upload is never refused at its end because somebody else sealed a version meanwhile. It stays open for a day, and
each part can be sent again. Past a limit (uploads open at once, uploads started in an hour, and the organisation's own limits on the largest
file, the files kept while they wait and the amount brought in a day) the answer is 429 with the seconds to wait.

Take one upload out of the pending set, without erasing that it arrived.

The row stays, so the ledger continues to show the file was uploaded and by
whom it was withdrawn. Deleting it would leave no answer to "what happened
to that file", which is the question somebody asks precisely when a
file has gone missing.

Withdrawing twice is not an error. The second call finds the row already
withdrawn and reports the same result, because the caller's intent is
already satisfied.
